payload.pattern: postgres-partial-index-immutable-rollback
payload.context: A partial-index predicate that calls a non-IMMUTABLE function can abort CREATE INDEX and roll back the entire surrounding migration transaction, leaving earlier statements and the migration ledger unapplied even when logs make progress look partial.
payload.solution: Preflight every partial-index predicate for volatility before apply; keep risky DDL isolated; after apply verify both intended objects and the exact migration-ledger row before claiming success. Treat one invalid predicate as transaction-wide failure, never as a local index miss.

payload.pattern: provenance-vs-claims-gate-classification
payload.summary: A truth gate that byte-compares a derived artifact cannot distinguish a recompute from a regression, so it reddens on every scheduled refresh and trains its operators to ignore it. Fix by CLASSIFICATION, never tolerance: enumerate claim-bearing fields and provenance-bearing fields separately, compare claims exactly, and let the verdict carry the distinction (identical / provenance-only / values-changed / missing). Do NOT compare with a tolerance and do NOT strip timestamps before comparing - both let a real regression through. Ship a witness asserting every field on the LIVE artifact falls into one of the two sets, or a future claim-bearing field is silently exempted and the gate rots into vacuity.

payload.pattern: recorded-fix-direction-is-a-hypothesis
payload.summary: A fix direction written into your own task board is a hypothesis, not a spec. Measure it before implementing it. StatVault S267: the board attributed a month-long red lane to two drifted franchise codes and prescribed a two-rule mapping; measuring the live source against the committed corpus found a THIRD code the board never named, used by only one of four feeds. Implementing the recorded prescription as written would have turned the lane green while leaving 13 already-committed rows wrong - a green gate over a wrong corpus, which is worse than a red one. Every mapping rule now carries the measurement that produced it.
payload.corollary: Normalise at the PRODUCER, never by widening the consumer gate. Teaching the integrity check that two codes are equivalent silences the error and destroys the very distinction the check exists to preserve.

payload.pattern: corpus-repair-must-assert-its-blast-radius
payload.summary: A script that rewrites a committed data artifact must prove what it changed BEFORE writing. StatVault S267 repaired 13 wrong strings and re-emitted single-line minified JSON profiles pretty-printed - ~1,500 changed lines per file to correct one string, burying the fix and destroying the review surface. Reverted, not shipped. The guard is cheap and exact: assert the byte delta equals the sum of the intended string-length changes, and refuse to write otherwise. The diff is huge but the content is fine is a claim no reviewer can check.

payload.topWin: The defect was invisible to every instrument pointed at it. F1–F6 read the working tree and F7 reads write-back currency; all seven said "not cut off", and they were right — the code WAS committed and pushed. What never happened was the ceremony that guards the commit. I found it by asking a question no probe asks: *which commit last touched this file, and does that match who should have touched it?* `PROJECT_STATUS.json`'s newest toucher was a hand-written `feat` commit, and the `chore` commit that should have carried the autopilot's writes contained three unrelated files. Two sessions of thirteen ruled gates, silently skipped, with a symptom (`lastSession` frozen at 280) sitting on the startup brief the whole time — un-owned, because the probe that detected it was the one probe in the fleet with no owner. Ruling a gate mandatory and proving it ran are different acts.
payload.topGap: I wrote a test file that reported **8/8 ✓ while silently skipping six tests I had just written**, because I appended them after the harness's `run()` call. I caught it only by counting `test(` declarations against the reported total — and I was, at that moment, in the middle of building a detector for greens that omit work. Two sessions running, the same shape has bitten me from a different angle: S282's shell heredoc ate text out of a source comment, and this session I used heredocs again for generated prose despite [SIL][S282 #1] committing me not to. The rule I keep re-learning is that a reported number is a claim, including when the number is mine and the claim is about my own work. Swept all 445 test files afterward and found no other instance, so the class is closed here — but the habit that produced it is not. And it happened a second time in the same session, through a different instrument: my red-detection grep anchored on `^\[[0-9]` while the runner prints `[ 50/458]` with a leading space, so I reported "3 failing, all mine" and twice said "clean so far" while `workflow-manifest-truth` was red in **all three** full runs. It was the one failure I had NOT caused — S282-era manifest drift hiding in that session's 144 budget-deferred files — and my filter was precisely the wrong shape to see it. Both lapses have the identical structure as the defects I spent the session fixing: a measurement that omits work while reporting success.

payload.pattern: skill-outcome
A ruled gate with no execution receipt is unenforceable — and tree-based triage cannot see a skipped ceremony
payload.solution: studio-ops S283: closeout-autopilot.mjs (13 ruled closeout gates) did not run for TWO consecutive sessions and nothing could tell. Every triage signal was correct and still blind: they read the working tree and write-back currency, but the code HAD been committed and pushed — what never ran was the ceremony guarding the commit. Found only by git archaeology: which commit last touched this file, and should it have? Fix: lib/closeout-receipt.mjs writes one NDJSON row per invocation, flushed on process EXIT so an ABORT (a gate refusing = the net working) is recorded as faithfully as a completion; a --dry-run receipt is explicitly NOT evidence. The consuming probe reports pre-instrument sessions as unprovable, never as bypasses — unknown is not disproven, and a gate nobody can clear gets disabled. Known limit, stated not hidden: an exit-flushed receipt lands after the run own git add, so a run cannot commit its own receipt.

payload.pattern: A bounded test run is not a green, and it must never retire a red
payload.solution: studio-ops S283: PROJECT_STATUS held testsPassing 384 / testsTotal 384 / testsDeferred [] and every founder surface rendered a checkmark — while two fields BELOW it in the same file recorded 30 budget-deferred files not counted green. The deferral lived only in prose that nothing parses. Worse, the empty array let the partial run count as a clean supersession and dismiss a genuine assertion-level red produced by a run that HAD executed those files, so the signal could not go red no matter how many files were skipped. Fix both halves: the reader gains a bounded state (never green, never supersedes a red) derived from run-mode and note as well as the array; the WRITER is checked at the status write path. Make that writer violation deliberately UNFIXABLE by --fix: the honest deferred-file list is knowable only to the run that skipped them, and fabricating entries to clear a CANON-031 check is the exact lie the check exists to catch. Also: every consumer enumerating known states falls through to green for a new one — put severity in the library and fail CLOSED on unrecognised states.

payload.pattern: An anchor-relative denominator launders all debt older than its anchor
payload.context: Any gate that computes its population as everything-since-the-last-checkpoint. check-writeback-currency.mjs (propagated to every Studio repo) uses debt = commits.slice(0, anchorIdx) where anchorIdx is the newest SELF_IMPROVEMENT_LOOP.md commit, so the moment ANY later closeout runs, every earlier un-written-back session leaves the denominator permanently. Measured live in obelisk at S254: the probe printed a PASS while S249 and S251 had shipped 12 commits with zero references across all eight state surfaces. Surface-vs-surface coherence probes cannot see it either, because the surfaces agree with each other and are all equally wrong.
payload.solution: Measure the whole population, derived from the artefact, instead of a suffix. obelisk shipped scripts/check-session-record-census.mjs: the session-label population comes from commit subjects on the release branch (the write side cannot free-string past a required commit subject), each label is RECORDED / UNRECORDED / RECEIPT-ONLY / EXCLUDED-with-a-reason, a declared VOID contradicted by git fails, and an empty population is UNMEASURED rather than a vacuous pass. Two calibration lessons: evidence must be a structural HEADING not any mention (the sentence explaining a session was missing cured its own alarm), and the detector must strip code spans or it reads its own documentation as a defect. Each false positive, once fixed, made the gate find MORE real debt.

payload.topWin: The session found the same defect wearing four different costumes — an instrument reading a *proxy* when a better source was sitting right there. A probe judged a receipt ledger by its commit message while the ledger recorded, in its own rows, exactly what the probe was trying to infer. A stranded-mail scan told you a cargo had no expiry while quoting a row that declared one. A cost alarm compared two windows without ever asking whether either contained real money. And the audit verifier accepted premises it had no adapter to read, then exited 0 and called the audit trustworthy — an audit made entirely of unreadable claims was indistinguishable from one that had been checked and held. None was a missing feature; each was a working instrument aimed at the weaker of two available sources, which is precisely the failure that survives review because every surface stays green. The generalisation is now a committed item: *is there an artifact that answers this probe's question more directly than the signal it reads?*
payload.topGap: I under-matched my own red-detection grep for the second session running. S283 recorded that its filter anchored on `^\[[0-9]` and missed a leading space; mine searched for `✗` while this runner marks reds with `⛔`, so I read "460 files, all ✓, 0 reds" off a run whose real exit code was 1, with both failures sitting in `.cache/test-failures.ndjson` the entire time. In the same session I also verified a fix with `node … | tail` and read *tail's* exit status as the command's — the exact trap the arc protocol warns about in writing, which I had read at the start of the session. Both are the same shape as the four defects I spent the session fixing: a measurement that omits work while reporting success. The rule is not "write better greps"; it is that a hand-written pattern over human-facing output is a guess about formatting, and the machine-readable sidecar was always there. Recorded as D-S284.6 so it is a practice rather than a third apology.
